/demo/founder-decision-review.h1: Should this company put another $120K into growth?
/demo/founder-decision-review.body:
This is the same deterministic engine behind every Quantis Decision Run — running on one fixed, fictional example. On the live page you move a slider and watch every dependent number recompute.

Illustrative Quantis demonstration. Values are a fixed example company, not a forecast for your business. Company: 420 existing customers, $300,000 starting cash, considering $120,000 in additional acquisition spend over months 1–3.

Break the model

The base case holds. Change one assumption and see what breaks it. The example assumptions:

  • Blended CAC: $1K
  • Monthly churn: 4.1%
  • Price / month: $149
  • Gross margin: 81%

Decision holds

  • Payback: Month 14
  • Lowest cash: $212K (month 3)

The chart on the live page shows cash with and without the investment, against a $175K cash floor.

What must be true for this to work?

Holding every other assumption at its current value, here is the boundary for each one.

  • Blended CAC: ≤ $1K
  • Monthly churn: ≤ 7.0%
  • Price / month: ≥ $121
  • Gross margin: ≥ 66%

Quantis does not make the decision for you. It shows what must be true for the decision to remain financially defensible.

/demo/hiring-decision.h1: Before the next hire, understand the cash commitment.
/demo/hiring-decision.body:
Can the business carry another employee before demand catches up? Payroll starts on day one; revenue only follows as new clients fill the new hours. Every number below comes from the same deterministic engine behind every Quantis Decision Run.

Interactive demo · illustrative example, not your business.

Illustrative example. A services business with 18 clients at $3,000/month, already at capacity (180 delivery hours = 18 clients), $60,000 in the bank. The hire adds 140 client hours per month (room for 14 more clients) and costs $4,000 up front to recruit and onboard. Decision rule: cash stays above $20,000 and the hire pays for itself within 12 months.

The example assumptions

  • New clients won per month: 1.5
  • Hire: fully loaded cost / month: $6,500
  • Clients pay after: 1 month
  • Gross margin on client work: 55%

To cover this hire alone at 55% margin, the business needs $11.8K of new revenue per month (≈ 3.9 clients): $6,500 ÷ 55%.

The business can carry this hire

  • Hire pays for itself: Month 11
  • Lowest cash: $40.0K (month 4)
  • New hours fully used: Month 14

Without the hire the team stays capped at 18 clients: new demand above that is not served.

What must be true for this hire to work?

Holding every other assumption at its current value, here is the boundary for each one.

  • New clients won per month: ≥ 1.3
  • Hire: fully loaded cost / month: ≤ $7,969
  • Clients pay after: ≤ 1 month
  • Gross margin on client work: ≥ 50%

Quantis does not make the hiring decision for you. It shows the cash commitment, how long payroll runs ahead of demand, and which assumption the decision depends on most. Your own numbers will differ from this example.

/demo/sample-decision-memo.h1: Should the firm hire one more delivery person now?
/demo/sample-decision-memo.body:
This is the shape of what a $349 Founder Decision Review delivers, worked through on a made-up services firm. The numbers are calculated by the same engine as the interactive hiring demo.

Fictional example. The business, owner and figures are invented to show the memo format. It is not a forecast, a client case or advice.

1. The decision

Hire one more delivery person at $6,500 a month fully loaded, plus $4,000 to recruit and onboard, or wait. The owner's rule: cash never drops below $20,000, and the hire pays for itself within 12 months.

2. Facts, assumptions and unknowns

Facts (supplied by the owner):

  • 18 clients at $3,000 a month
  • Team delivers 180 hours a month: full at 18 clients
  • $60,000 in the bank
  • Fixed costs $28,500 a month

Assumptions (estimates):

  • 1.5 new clients won per month
  • Clients pay 1 month after the work
  • Gross margin 55%
  • The hire adds 140 client hours a month
  • 2% of clients leave each month

Unknowns (not modeled):

  • How many weeks until the hire is fully productive
  • Whether demand holds past the first six months
  • Whether current clients would leave if service slips without the hire

3. Three scenarios

  • Downside: 0.75 new clients a month, paid 2 months after the work, 50% margin. Payback not within 18 months; lowest cash -$33,300 (month 18). Fails: cash falls below $20,000 in month 5; the hire never pays back within 18 months.
  • Base: 1.5 new clients a month, paid 1 month after the work, 55% margin. Payback month 11; lowest cash $39,957 (month 4). Holds.
  • Upside: 2.5 new clients a month, paid 1 month after the work, 58% margin. Payback month 7; lowest cash $47,020 (month 2). Holds.

4. Cash, break-even and payback, reconciled

  • To cover the hire alone, the firm needs $11,818 more revenue a month ($6,500 ÷ 55% margin), about 3.9 new clients at $3,000.
  • In the base case the hire's cumulative cash effect turns positive in month 11; the lowest balance is $39,957 in month 4.
  • In the downside, cash breaks the $20,000 floor in month 5: slower wins and later payment tie up cash while payroll runs from day one.

5. What would change the decision

Each line is the point where the base case stops meeting the owner's rule, holding everything else fixed.

  1. New clients won per month stay at or above 1.32 (assumed 1.5).
  2. The hire's fully loaded cost stays at or below $7,960 a month (assumed $6,500).
  3. Clients pay no later than 1 month after the work (assumed 1 month after the work). No slack: one month later breaks the rule.
  4. Gross margin on client work stays at or above 49.6% (assumed 55%).
  5. How fast the hire becomes productive. Not modeled here; in a real review it is asked at intake and tested as a scenario.

6. Conclusion

Conditional go. The hire meets the rule in the base and upside cases but not in the downside. Before committing, confirm the pipeline supports the new-client threshold above and that clients pay on current terms; review again after three months of actual wins.

Limitations: decision support based on supplied information and stated assumptions. Not accounting, tax, legal or investment advice, and not a guarantee of any outcome.

/demo/consultant-founding-pilot.h1: Your client says 30 new customers a month. Can you actually serve that many?
/demo/consultant-founding-pilot.body:
Same deterministic engine behind every Quantis Decision Run, applied to a services business with a fixed delivery capacity. On the live page you move a slider and watch the gap between claimed demand and real capacity recompute.

Illustrative Quantis demonstration. Values are a fixed example services business, not a forecast for your business. Company: 12 existing customers already consuming capacity, $165/mo average ticket, 58% gross margin.

Reconcile the claim

Change what the client claims, or what your team can actually deliver, and see where the story breaks. The example assumptions:

  • Client claims new customers / month: 30/mo
  • Hours to serve one customer / month: 52 hrs
  • Hours your team actually has / month: 1040 hrs

The claim exceeds real capacity

  • Max customers you can serve: 20
  • Hours short / month: 1144, including 12 existing customers

By month 12, the plan counts 314 customers but the team can only serve 20 — $49K in revenue this plan is counting on but cannot actually deliver.

Why this happens every time

A claimed growth number and your team's real delivery capacity are two different numbers, computed two different ways — nobody reconciles them until the customers show up. Quantis runs the reconciliation on the same engine as your P&L, every month, before you sign the engagement.

Quantis does not tell you to turn the client down. It shows exactly how much of the plan your current capacity cannot support.
